title: Demonstrate an understanding of agricultural production management practices in relation to the socio-economic environment

lessons.title: The farm and the world around it
lessons.html:
The farm and the world around it

A farm does not stand alone. What happens in the community, the country and the world affects how the farm works, and what the farm does affects the people around it. The socio-economic environment means the social things (people, community, culture, health, education) and the economic things (prices, jobs, money, markets) around the farm.

Economic things that affect the farm

  • Prices of inputs: when diesel, fertiliser or feed prices go up, it costs more to farm.
  • Prices of products: maize, meat or fruit prices go up and down. Low prices mean less money for the farm.
  • Interest rates: farms that borrow money pay more when interest rates rise.
  • The exchange rate: when the rand is weak, exported fruit earns more rand, but imported fertiliser and machinery cost more.
  • Electricity and water supply: load shedding and water shortages affect irrigation, cold rooms and milking.

Social things that affect the farm

  • Skills and education of workers.
  • Health of workers and families, for example HIV and TB, which affect people's ability to work.
  • Crime such as stock theft and theft of cables and equipment.
  • Housing, transport and services such as clinics and schools.
  • Relationships between the farm and the community.

Example

On a citrus farm near Kirkwood, the price of diesel and fertiliser went up, and load shedding made irrigation difficult. At the same time, the rand was weak, so export prices in rand were good. The manager had to balance higher costs against better income, and plan irrigation around power cuts.

lessons.title: Good management practices in the community
lessons.html:
Good management practices in the community

Good farm managers think about the socio-economic environment when they plan and run production. This helps the farm survive and improves life for workers and the community.

Practices that help the farm cope with economic changes

  • Planning and budgets: know costs and expected income before the season.
  • Saving inputs: use fertiliser, water, fuel and chemicals carefully, as instructed. Waste costs everyone.
  • Producing good quality: good quality gets better prices and keeps buyers.
  • More than one product or market: if one price falls, the others help.
  • Backup power and water plans for load shedding and drought.

Practices that build a good social environment

  • Fair labour practices: following labour laws on wages, hours, leave and contracts, such as the Basic Conditions of Employment Act.
  • Safe workplaces: following the OHS Act 85 of 1993.
  • Training and development: workers who learn skills earn more and do better work.
  • Health support: first aid, clean water, toilets, access to clinics, health education.
  • Good communication: worker committees, regular meetings, listening to problems.
  • Community links: buying locally, supporting schools, sharing information with small-scale farmers, working with neighbours on fire and crime prevention.

Caring for the environment

Pollution of rivers, soil erosion and veld fires hurt the community too. Farms must protect natural resources under laws such as the Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 and the National Water Act 36 of 1998.

What you can do

  1. Work safely and do quality work.
  2. Do not waste inputs, water or electricity.
  3. Report theft, damage and unsafe conditions.
  4. Take part in training and worker meetings.
  5. Respect your neighbours and the community.

Key points

  • The socio-economic environment is the social and economic world around the farm.
  • Input prices, product prices, interest rates, the exchange rate and electricity all affect the farm.
  • Skills, health, crime and community relations also affect production.
  • Good management plans for changes, saves inputs and produces quality.
  • Fair labour, safety, training and community links benefit the farm and the people.
